title: Radial nerve transection: impaired wrist extension
vignette: A 23-year-old man is brought to the emergency department after sustaining stab injuries in a street fight. The patient feels lightheaded and dizzy. Blood pressure is 100/60 mm Hg and pulse is 115/min. Physical examination shows profuse bleeding from penetrating wounds over the right neck and shoulder area. Intravenous fluids are administered, and a blood transfusion is initiated. Urgent surgical exploration is performed, and injured blood vessels are repaired. Further exploration shows complete transection of a specific nerve, indicated by an arrow on the brachial plexus diagram pointing to the radial nerve. Which of the following actions is most likely to be impaired as a result of this patient's nerve injury?

clues.text: penetrating wounds over the right neck and shoulder area
clues.note: A stab to the neck/shoulder can injure branches of the brachial plexus - the arrow identifies which nerve.

clues.text: complete transection of a specific nerve, indicated by an arrow on the brachial plexus diagram pointing to the radial nerve
clues.note: The arrowed nerve is the RADIAL nerve, which innervates the extensor compartment of the upper limb.

whatMatters: The transected (arrowed) nerve is the RADIAL NERVE, which innervates all the EXTENSOR muscles of the arm and forearm. Radial nerve injury therefore impairs WRIST (and finger) EXTENSION - producing 'wrist drop.' Answer C.
strategy: Identify the radial nerve, then recall its motor function: extensors of the wrist and fingers (plus triceps and supinator); sensory to the posterior arm/forearm and dorsal lateral hand. Injury -> wrist drop (impaired wrist extension). Reject actions of other nerves: finger abduction (ulnar - interossei), thumb adduction (ulnar), wrist flexion (median/ulnar), and thumb opposition (median - recurrent branch).

eliminations.label: Finger abduction - ulnar nerve (dorsal interossei)
eliminations.detail: WHAT IT IS: spreading the fingers, performed by the dorsal interossei (ULNAR nerve). ❌ WHY IT FAILS: that's an ulnar-nerve action, not radial. ✅ Correct if: ulnar nerve injury (weak finger abduction, claw hand).

eliminations.label: Thumb adduction - ulnar nerve (adductor pollicis)
eliminations.detail: WHAT IT IS: adductor pollicis (ULNAR nerve) pulling the thumb toward the palm. ❌ WHY IT FAILS: ulnar, not radial. ✅ Correct if: ulnar nerve injury (positive Froment sign).

eliminations.label: Wrist flexion - median/ulnar nerves
eliminations.detail: WHAT IT IS: wrist flexors (flexor carpi radialis - median; flexor carpi ulnaris - ulnar). ❌ WHY IT FAILS: those are median/ulnar-innervated flexors, not the radial-innervated extensors. ✅ Correct if: median or ulnar injury affecting flexion.

eliminations.label: Thumb opposition - median nerve (recurrent branch)
eliminations.detail: WHAT IT IS: opponens pollicis (MEDIAN recurrent branch) rotating the thumb to oppose. ❌ WHY IT FAILS: that's a median-nerve (thenar) function, not radial. ✅ Correct if: median nerve/carpal tunnel injury (weak opposition, thenar atrophy).

reasoning: The arrowed nerve on the brachial plexus is the radial nerve
The radial nerve innervates all extensor muscles of the arm and forearm
Radial nerve transection impairs wrist (and finger) extension = wrist drop
-> extension of the wrist; answer C
mechanism: The RADIAL NERVE is the largest branch of the brachial plexus (from the posterior cord, C5-T1). It innervates ALL the EXTENSOR muscles of the upper limb below the shoulder - triceps (elbow extension), and the wrist and finger extensors and supinator in the forearm - and provides sensation to the posterior arm/forearm and the dorsal lateral hand. It courses in the radial groove of the humerus (vulnerable to midshaft humeral fractures) and superficially in the axilla (vulnerable to penetrating wounds, as here). Injury to the radial nerve causes weakness of wrist and finger EXTENSION - the classic 'WRIST DROP' - with variable posterior-arm/forearm sensory loss (a proximal lesion also weakens elbow extension). Therefore transection impairs wrist extension. The distractor movements are performed by ULNAR-innervated muscles (finger abduction via dorsal interossei; thumb adduction via adductor pollicis), MEDIAN/ulnar wrist FLEXORS, and the MEDIAN nerve's thenar opponens (thumb opposition).

difficulty.label: 🧠 Knowledge
difficulty.text: First Aid Anatomy > radial nerve (posterior cord, C5-T1): all extensors (triceps, wrist/finger extensors, supinator); sensory posterior arm/dorsal hand; injury -> wrist drop (radial groove/axilla).

difficulty.label: 📖 Comprehension
difficulty.text: Radial nerve = extensors, so its transection impairs wrist extension (wrist drop).

difficulty.label: 🔤 Vocab
difficulty.text: Unsure on radial nerve, wrist drop, extensor compartment, posterior cord, or interossei? Tell me which.

difficulty.label: 🨤 Distractor
difficulty.text: Finger abduction/thumb adduction = ulnar; wrist flexion = median/ulnar; thumb opposition = median (thenar).

difficulty.label: 🖼️ Imaging / diagram
difficulty.text: On the brachial plexus diagram: the arrow points to the RADIAL nerve arising from the posterior cord. Anchor: 'radial nerve = extensors = wrist drop.'

difficulty.label: 🗒️ Other
difficulty.text: Bank: radial nerve = extensors (wrist drop); midshaft humerus/axilla injury; posterior cord (C5-T1).

firstAid.detail: Anatomy: extensors -> wrist drop when injured; posterior cord.
Anatomy > radial injury at humeral midshaft/axilla.

memoryHook: Radial nerve = the 'extensor' nerve; cut it and the wrist flops into a drop - the extensors that hold the hand up go dark.
